name: Marpha
tagline: Whitewashed lanes, apple orchards and a gompa above the roofs
meta_description: Marpha in Lower Mustang: the stone-paved Thakali village known for apples and apple brandy, its Nyingma gompa, Chhairo and the walk from Jomsom.
summary: Marpha is a Thakali village at about 2,670 m, two hours' walk south of Jomsom on the Kali Gandaki. It is known across Nepal for apples, apple brandy and dried fruit, and for its whitewashed, stone-paved main lane with flat-roofed houses and covered drains. A calmer overnight stop than Jomsom.
intro: Marpha is the village most people picture when they think of Lower Mustang. A single paved lane runs between whitewashed houses with flat roofs and dark wooden windows. Water runs in a channel under the paving stones. Firewood is stacked along the rooftops, and in autumn the roofs and courtyards are covered with apples, apricots and buckwheat laid out to dry. Above it all, the red and white Nyingma gompa looks down the valley towards Dhaulagiri.

This is the apple capital of Nepal. Orchards cover the terraces on both sides of the river, and almost every lodge sells apple pie, apple juice, dried apple rings and the local apple brandy. The fruit trade began with a government horticulture farm set up in the 1960s, and Marpha's growers now send truckloads to Pokhara and Kathmandu each autumn. September and October are harvest months, the best time to come.

We like Marpha as an overnight stop instead of Jomsom. It is quieter, the lodges are family-run and the walk in, two hours along the river from Jomsom, is the right length for an acclimatisation day. It also makes a good base for the Tibetan settlement and gompa at Chhairo across the river, and for the walk on to Tukuche, the old salt-trade village a little further south. One night is usually enough.

story.title: The hard-working people of the apple village
paras: Marpha's name is often explained as 'mar', hard-working, and 'pha', people, and the village has earned it. Its families, the Marphali, are one of the four groups who call themselves Thakali. Their clans carry the surnames Hirachan, Pannachan, Jwarchan and Lalchan. Like the other Thakali villages of the Kali Gandaki, Marpha prospered from trade along the river, as caravans moved Tibetan salt and wool south and grain and goods north, and its houses were built for a valley where the wind blows every afternoon.

In 1899 the Japanese monk Ekai Kawaguchi came up the Kali Gandaki looking for a way into Tibet, which was closed to foreigners. He spent months in Mustang, studying in Tsarang and then living in Marpha, before slipping across a high pass into Tibet in 1900. He was the first recorded Japanese citizen to travel to Nepal or Tibet, and his book Three Years in Tibet describes the Kali Gandaki villages as they were in the last years of the 19th century.

When the salt trade declined in the mid-20th century, Marpha turned to fruit. A government horticulture farm in the 1960s introduced improved apple varieties suited to the cold, dry climate. Orchards replaced some barley fields, and the village began distilling apple brandy. Today tourism and fruit carry most households. Many younger Marphali live in Pokhara or Kathmandu for school and work, but families return for harvest and for festivals, when the gompa is full and the lane is crowded again.

legend: Villagers tell a story about the chorten painted on the cliff above the gompa. Long ago, they say, Marpha was struck by leprosy and nothing the people tried could stop it. A monk from Tukuche, the village to the south, told them to build a chorten on the rock face and hold rituals there. They did as he said, the sickness ended, and Marpha prospered again. The painted chorten and the small stone chortens on the ledges below it are still looked after today.
people: Marpha's families are Marphali Thakali, with their own clan names and customs, and Thakali is still spoken at home alongside Nepali. Most households combine orchards, lodges and trade; some still keep mules and horses. Across the river at Chhairo lives a Tibetan community settled after 1959, many of whom run souvenir stalls in Marpha's lane. Religious life centres on the Nyingma gompa, with Thakali clan rituals alongside.

untold.fact: Marpha's main lane has a covered drainage system running beneath the stone paving, which carries water through the village. It is one reason the village has long been praised as a model of traditional planning in the Kali Gandaki valley.

Chhairo, on the opposite bank of the Kali Gandaki just south of Marpha, has the first Nyingma monastery established in Mustang district, and a Tibetan refugee settlement whose residents run many of the craft stalls in Marpha.
The Japanese monk Ekai Kawaguchi lived in Marpha in 1899–1900 while preparing to cross secretly into Tibet, after studying Buddhism in Tsarang in Upper Mustang.
untold.source: Embassy of Japan in Nepal: Ekai Kawaguchi

local_words.meaning: distilled spirit; in Marpha usually made from apples
monastery or temple; Marpha's sits above the village

taste.name: Marpha apple brandy
taste.text: Marpha's apple brandy is a clear or pale-gold spirit distilled from local apples, sometimes from apricots too. Lodges along the main lane serve it by the glass and sell sealed bottles. Pair it with apple pie or dried apple rings, and try it after dinner, not before a pass.

facts: ≈ 355 km · 2 days by road; flight to Jomsom then 20 min by jeep
Apples, apple brandy, whitewashed Thakali lanes, Nyingma gompa

highlights.title: The paved main lane
highlights.text: Walk the length of Marpha's stone-flagged lane in the early morning, when the light comes down the valley and the wind has not started. Notice the water channel beneath your feet, the wooden window frames and the firewood stacked along the rooftops.

highlights.title: Marpha gompa and the painted chorten
highlights.text: Climb the steps to the Nyingma gompa above the village for a view over the flat roofs to the Kali Gandaki and Dhaulagiri. Above it, a chorten is painted on the cliff, tied to the village's leprosy legend.

highlights.title: Apple harvest
highlights.text: September and October are harvest months. Orchards are heavy with fruit, apples dry on every roof and you can buy juice, jam, cider and brandy straight from the families who make them. It is the best time to stay overnight.

highlights.title: Chhairo and its gompa
highlights.text: Cross the river south of the village to Chhairo, with its Tibetan settlement and the first Nyingma monastery in Mustang. A quiet hour's walk, and a chance to meet Tibetan families who have lived here since the 1960s.

highlights.title: The walk from Jomsom
highlights.text: Two hours down the Kali Gandaki from Jomsom on a riverside trail, with Nilgiri behind you and Dhaulagiri ahead. Start early to walk with the wind at your back, or take a jeep for 20 minutes if time is short.

how_to_reach.text: Marpha is on the Beni–Jomsom road, ≈ 6 km south of Jomsom (about 20 minutes by jeep) and ≈ 155 km from Pokhara (7–8 hours by jeep). Buses between Jomsom and Beni stop on the main road just below the village.
The nearest airport is Jomsom, with early-morning flights from Pokhara of about 20 minutes. From the airport, take a jeep or walk two hours south along the river.

On the Annapurna Circuit or the Kali Gandaki trail, Marpha is a two-hour walk from Jomsom and about two hours from Tukuche. Trekkers coming down from Muktinath often spend their first night below the pass here.

where_to_stay: Marpha has around a dozen family-run lodges along the paved lane and on the road below, most with heated dining rooms, attached bathrooms in the better rooms and kitchens that make their own apple dishes. They are simple but clean; we pick lodges where the family still lives on site. There is no high-end hotel in the village. For more comfort, stay at Shinta Mani Mustang or Om's Home in Jomsom, 20 minutes away by jeep, and visit Marpha as a half-day walk.
tips: Walk from Jomsom in the morning; the afternoon wind blows up the valley into your face.
Buy dried apples and brandy here rather than in Jomsom; you buy direct from the families who make them.
Remove shoes and hats inside the gompa and walk clockwise around chortens and prayer wheels.
Ask before photographing people working in courtyards or on rooftops, especially older women.
If you are carrying on over the Thorong La in reverse, do not drink brandy the night before climbing.

experiences.title: Apple orchards and the brandy of Marpha
experiences.summary: Walk the orchards on the terraces around Marpha with a local grower, see how apples are dried on the rooftops and pressed for juice, and taste the apple brandy, cider and jam that have made this village famous across Nepal.
body: Marpha's apples grow on irrigated terraces on both sides of the Kali Gandaki, protected from the wind by stone walls and lines of poplar and willow. We start with a walk through the orchards with a grower, who explains how the varieties introduced by the government horticulture farm in the 1960s were adapted to cold winters and dry summers. Harvest runs from late August into October. Some trees in the oldest orchards are now more than 50 years old.

Back in the village, the fruit is sorted in courtyards. The best apples are packed for trucks to Pokhara and Kathmandu; smaller ones are cut into rings and dried on the rooftops, pressed for juice or fermented for cider and brandy. In some houses you can see the copper or steel stills used for distilling. Each family has its own recipe and strength. Nothing is wasted: peel and cores go to the animals.

We finish with a tasting in a family lodge: fresh juice, a slice of apple pie, dried fruit and a small glass of brandy for those who want it. Bottles are sold sealed and pack well. Remember that alcohol and altitude do not mix; if you are heading higher the next day, keep the tasting small or save it for the way down. We can also arrange a box of fresh apples to be sent down to your Pokhara hotel in season.

faqs.q: When is apple season in Marpha?
faqs.a: Apples ripen from late August and harvest continues through September and into October, with the peak usually in September. This is when orchards are full, roofs are covered with drying fruit and fresh juice is everywhere. Dried apples and brandy are sold all year, but come in September or early October for the harvest itself.

faqs.q: Can I bring Marpha brandy home?
faqs.a: Yes. Sealed bottles of Marpha apple brandy are sold in the village and in Jomsom and travel well in checked luggage. Small planes from Jomsom have strict weight limits, so remember bottles are heavy. Your home country's duty-free allowance applies when you arrive. Do not carry open bottles in hand luggage on flights.

faqs.q: Is the apple orchard visit suitable for children?
faqs.a: Yes. The orchard walk is flat or gently sloping and short, and children usually enjoy picking up fallen apples, seeing fruit dry on the roofs and drinking fresh juice. The brandy tasting is for adults only. Bring sun hats and warm layers, since the afternoon wind can be cold even in September.

experiences.title: Marpha gompa and the whitewashed lanes
experiences.summary: A slow walk through Marpha's paved lanes and up to its Nyingma gompa, with a guide who explains Thakali house design, the covered drains, the rooftop firewood and the legend of the chorten painted on the cliff above the village.
body: We start at the southern end of the village where the main lane begins. The stone paving covers a drainage channel that carries water through Marpha, an old solution in a valley where every drop is managed. Houses face inwards onto courtyards to escape the wind, with flat roofs used for drying crops and for storing firewood. Your guide will explain how the size of a family's woodpile was long read as a sign of its standing.

Halfway along, steps lead up to the Nyingma gompa. Morning prayers sometimes take place early, and you are welcome to sit quietly at the back. Inside are statues of Guru Rinpoche and other Nyingma figures, painted walls and butter lamps. From the courtyard the view runs over the flat roofs to the river and the snow of Dhaulagiri and Tukuche Peak. Look for the old wooden prayer wheel by the entrance, turned by every villager who passes.

Above the gompa a chorten is painted on the cliff face, with small stone chortens on the ledges below. Villagers link it to a time when Marpha was struck by leprosy and a monk from Tukuche told them to build it. We walk back down through the northern lanes, past prayer wheels and kani gates, and finish with tea in a family kitchen. Take your time on the way down; the side lanes are where you see daily life.

faqs.q: Can visitors enter Marpha monastery?
faqs.a: Yes, visitors are generally welcome in Marpha's gompa outside private rituals. Remove shoes and hats, walk clockwise, do not touch statues or offerings, and ask before taking photographs inside. A small donation in the box is appreciated. If prayers are in progress, sit quietly at the back or come back later.

faqs.q: What Buddhist school is Marpha gompa?
faqs.a: Marpha's main gompa belongs to the Nyingma school, the oldest of the four main Tibetan Buddhist schools, which traces itself to Guru Rinpoche (Padmasambhava). Across the river, Chhairo gompa is also Nyingma and is described as the first Nyingma monastery established in Mustang district.

faqs.q: How long does it take to see Marpha village?
faqs.a: The lanes and the gompa take about 1.5 hours at an easy pace, longer if you stop for photographs or tea. Add an hour for Chhairo across the river and a couple of hours for an orchard visit. One night in Marpha gives you a relaxed evening and early-morning light in the lanes.

experiences.title: Chhairo gompa and the Tibetan settlement
experiences.summary: Cross the Kali Gandaki south of Marpha to Chhairo, home to a Tibetan settlement founded after 1959 and to the first Nyingma monastery in Mustang. A short, quiet walk with weaving, prayer wheels and a gompa that has been carefully restored.
body: From the southern end of Marpha we walk down to the river and cross to the east bank, about 30–40 minutes on a level path through orchards. Chhairo sits among fields and willows, a small cluster of houses, chortens and prayer walls. It is easy to miss from the main road, and most trekkers walk straight past. Willows and poplars shelter the fields here, and the light in the morning is soft and low across the river.

Chhairo's gompa is described as the first Nyingma monastery established in Mustang district. Its old wall paintings are worth seeing slowly, with a torch. Ask your guide to find the caretaker if the door is locked. Nearby lives a Tibetan community that settled here after 1959; some families weave carpets and run the souvenir stalls you will see in Marpha. The gompa is small, so allow 20–30 minutes inside and keep a torch handy for the darker corners.

We return along the east bank and recross to Marpha, or carry on south towards Tukuche if you are walking down the valley. Chhairo is quiet and residential, so keep voices low, ask before photographing people and buy something small if you visit a workshop. Mornings are calmest; the afternoon wind on the open riverbed can be hard going. A walk here pairs well with the orchard visit later in the day.

faqs.q: How do I get to Chhairo from Marpha?
faqs.a: Walk south from Marpha to the river and cross to the east bank; Chhairo is about 30–40 minutes from the village on a level path. Your guide will know the current crossing point, which can change after the monsoon. Allow about two hours for the round trip with time at the gompa and in the settlement.

faqs.q: Who lives in Chhairo?
faqs.a: Chhairo is home to Tibetan families who settled in Mustang after 1959, alongside a small number of local households. Many Tibetans here make a living from trade, weaving and running souvenir stalls in Marpha. It is a residential place, not a tourist site, so walk quietly and ask before taking photographs.

faqs.q: Is there an entry fee for Chhairo gompa?
faqs.a: There is usually no fixed ticket, but a donation is expected and goes towards upkeep and the caretaker. Leave NPR 200–500 in the donation box. If the gompa is locked, your guide can usually find the keyholder in the settlement. Remove shoes before entering and ask before photographing inside.

experiences.title: Walk the Kali Gandaki from Jomsom to Marpha
experiences.summary: An easy half-day walk south along the Kali Gandaki from Jomsom to Marpha, with Nilgiri behind and Dhaulagiri ahead, on old trading trails and village paths away from the jeep road. A good first walk in Mustang.
body: We leave Jomsom after breakfast and walk south along the west bank, then follow paths that keep off the jeep road where they can. The valley is broad here, with gravel flats and braided channels of the Kali Gandaki. Behind you Nilgiri stands above Jomsom; ahead, Dhaulagiri and Tukuche Peak fill the view as you descend gently, about 30 m of height loss over 6 km. Most of the walk is on flat or gently falling ground.

Along the way are the orchards and fields of Syang, one of the Teen Gaunle Thakali villages, and the old trail used for centuries by mule and yak caravans carrying salt and grain. Your guide will point out the old chortens, the irrigation channels and the dry hillsides where blue sheep sometimes come down to graze in winter. Stop for tea in Syang if you want a break; it is roughly halfway.

We reach Marpha in about two hours, in time for lunch and an afternoon in the orchards or at the gompa. If the wind has started early, it will be at your back on this direction of walk, one reason we prefer it to the uphill direction. Luggage goes by jeep, so you only carry a daypack with water, sunscreen and a windproof. In winter, start a little later, once the sun has reached the valley floor.

faqs.q: How long is the walk from Jomsom to Marpha?
faqs.a: It is about 6 km and takes 2–2.5 hours at an easy pace, with very little climbing; the trail loses a little height going south. It is one of the easiest walks in Mustang and suits most fitness levels. Start in the morning so the afternoon wind does not catch you, and send luggage ahead by jeep.

faqs.q: Is the Jomsom–Marpha walk on the road?
faqs.a: Partly. The jeep road runs down the valley, but good guides use village paths, riverbank trails and sections of the old caravan route to keep you off it for much of the way. Dust from passing vehicles is the main nuisance, so carry a buff. In the monsoon, river-level paths may be flooded.

faqs.q: Can I walk from Marpha to Tukuche as well?
faqs.a: Yes. Tukuche is about 7 km further south, roughly 2 hours on a similar easy trail, passing Chhairo on the opposite bank. Many people walk Jomsom–Marpha one day and Marpha–Tukuche the next, staying a night in each, which makes a relaxed two-day introduction to Thakali villages.

faqs.q: Is Marpha worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes. Marpha is the best-preserved Thakali village in the Kali Gandaki valley that is easy to reach, with a paved lane, whitewashed houses, a Nyingma gompa and apple orchards. It is quieter than Jomsom and has good family lodges. Spend one night here, or at least visit on a half-day walk from Jomsom.

faqs.q: How far is Marpha from Jomsom?
faqs.a: Marpha is about 6 km south of Jomsom. It takes about 20 minutes by jeep on the Beni–Jomsom road, or 2–2.5 hours on foot along the river. Most visitors walk one way and drive the other, or walk in and stay the night. Jeeps can be arranged in Jomsom for a half-day return trip.

faqs.q: What is Marpha famous for?
faqs.a: Marpha is famous for apples and apple products: brandy, juice, cider, jam and dried apple rings, sold all over Nepal. It is also known for its stone-paved main lane with a covered drain beneath, whitewashed flat-roofed Thakali houses, and its Nyingma gompa overlooking the valley.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Marpha?
faqs.a: September and October are best, with apple harvest, clear skies and comfortable days around 15–20 °C. March to May is also good, with blossom in April. Winter is sunny but cold, with nights well below freezing. The monsoon brings little rain here, but roads and flights from Pokhara can be disrupted.

faqs.q: Can I stay overnight in Marpha?
faqs.a: Yes. Marpha has around a dozen family-run lodges, most with heated dining rooms and some with attached bathrooms. They are simple but comfortable. There is no high-end hotel here; for that, stay in Jomsom and visit Marpha by day. We book lodges where the family lives on site and cooks fresh.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to visit Marpha?
faqs.a: Yes. Marpha is inside the Annapurna Conservation Area, so foreigners need an ACAP permit (NPR 3,000; SAARC nationals NPR 1,000) and a TIMS card. Since April 2023 foreign trekkers in conservation areas need a licensed guide. No restricted area permit is needed for Marpha. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Who are the people of Marpha?
faqs.a: Marpha's people are Marphali, one of four groups who identify as Thakali. Their clan names include Hirachan, Pannachan, Jwarchan and Lalchan. They speak Thakali at home and Nepali widely, and follow Tibetan Buddhism alongside their own clan rituals. A Tibetan community lives across the river at Chhairo.

faqs.q: Is Marpha on the Annapurna Circuit?
faqs.a: Yes. Marpha lies on the Kali Gandaki section of the Annapurna Circuit, below Jomsom. Trekkers coming down from the Thorong La and Muktinath often stay here. Today many people take a jeep after Jomsom, but walking from Jomsom to Marpha and Tukuche on the quieter side trails is still worthwhile.

faqs.q: How cold is Marpha at night?
faqs.a: In October and April, nights fall to around 0–5 °C and days reach 15–20 °C. From December to February, nights can drop to −8 °C or lower, with sunny but cold days. Lodges heat the dining room in the evening; bedrooms are often unheated, so bring a warm sleeping bag or ask for extra blankets.
